In December 1936 he would stage the Xi’an Incident, seizing Chiang Kai-shek to force a united front against Japan, and pass the next half-century under house arrest. Du’s arranging his cure is of a piece with the broker’s role this chapter describes.

ch17.anchor: Shi Liangcai came to the Du house almost daily
ch17.note: Shi Liangcai (史量才, 1880–1934), proprietor of the Shenbao, Shanghai’s leading daily, whose increasingly independent line angered the Nationalist government. He was shot dead near Hangzhou in November 1934 by agents widely understood to be acting on Chiang Kai-shek’s orders — which gives an edge to the narrator’s remark that Du grieved for days.

ch17.anchor: the so-called "three elders" among the traitors
ch17.note: The ‘three elders’ (三老) were three senior figures of the Shanghai business and civic establishment — Wen Lanting, Lin Kanghou and Yuan Lüdeng — who took office under the Japanese-sponsored puppet municipal administration during the occupation and were prosecuted as collaborators (汉奸, ‘traitors to the Han’) after 1945.

Du’s children are enumerated differently by different memoirists. The household accountant Huang Guodong (ch. 16) names eight sons — Weifan, Weiyuan, Weihan, Weining, Weiping, Weixin, Weishan and Weisong — with no ‘Weiren’ among them, and gives Weifan as the son of Du’s first wife, née Shen, not of ‘Lao Si.’ Yu Yongfu’s list is followed here as printed; the discrepancy is the two witnesses’.

The source glosses the transliterated maidamu (麦达姆) as English for ‘mother,’ but the word is Madam(e): what Meng Xiaodong was pressing for was recognition as Du’s wife and mistress of the house, not a form of address. Du married her, at last, only on the eve of leaving for Hong Kong.

ch18.note: The phrase san yang kai tai (三阳开泰) — ‘three suns usher in prosperity’ — is a stock New Year auspicious saying. Here it is a pun: the yang of ‘sun’ (阳) is a homophone of the surname Yang (杨), so that the three ‘suns’ are Du’s three Yang advisers, Yang Du, Yang Zhixiong, and Yang Guanbei.

Zhang Jian (张謇, 1853–1926) placed first in the palace examination of 1894, highest of all the empire’s scholars; but instead of an official’s career he turned to industry, building at his native Nantong the Dasheng cotton mills, salt-reclamation companies, schools, and the Dada shipping lines, and became the very model of the reform-minded gentry-entrepreneur of the late Qing and early Republic. The zhuangyuan was the scholar ranked first in the whole realm at the triennial palace examination.

ch18.anchor: the May Third Incident occurred at Jinan
ch18.note: The narrator dates this to 1927, but the Jinan Incident (the ‘May Third Incident,’ 五三惨案) took place on 3 May 1928, when Japanese troops clashed with the Northern Expeditionary army at Jinan and killed thousands; the boycott of Japanese goods that followed is what this chapter goes on to describe. The year is the source’s slip.

Li Gongpu (李公朴, 1902–1946), later a well-known educator and campaigner for democracy; his assassination by Nationalist secret agents at Kunming in 1946, days before that of the poet Wen Yiduo, caused a national outcry. Here he appears as a young army liaison officer.

ch18.anchor: Zhu was the bishop of Haimen
ch18.note: Lu Bohong (陆伯鸿) and Zhu Zhiyao (朱志尧) were the foremost Catholic industrialists of Shanghai, and Lu was indeed made a papal knight. But Zhu Zhiyao was a layman, not a bishop: the first Chinese bishop of Haimen was his kinsman Zhu Kaimin (朱开敏), consecrated in 1926. The narrator has run the two together.

ch18.anchor: a case of "the magistrate may burn down houses, but the common folk may not so much as light a lamp."
ch18.note: A proverb for one law for the powerful and another for the people. It comes from a Song tale of a prefect named Tian Deng (田登) who, to taboo his own name, forbade the townsfolk the word deng, ‘lamp’ (a homophone), so that the lantern-festival proclamation had to announce ‘the lighting of fire’ instead.

This is the launch called the Yuebao (月宝) in the preceding chapter’s account of the Du ancestral-temple dedication, where Yu Yongfu, the opium-pipe attendant, lists it among Du’s two motor-launches. Huang Zhendong’s gift is thus how one of them came to be built.

ch18.anchor: played the black-faced villains and Du Yuesheng the white-faced one
ch18.note: The image is from opera face-painting: a black face marks the fierce or brutal role, a white face the crafty and treacherous one. Chen Qun and Yang Hu did the menacing and Du the smiling settlement — the good-cop, bad-cop division of a shakedown.

ch19.note: Two rural counties on the eastern edge of greater Shanghai (Chuansha lies in what is now Pudong). That the narrator held the electric-power franchise in both marks him as a man of provincial capital and standing, not a mere exchange functionary.

ch19.anchor: the Chicago telegram on American wheat
ch19.note: China's mechanized flour mills ran largely on imported wheat — American, Australian, Canadian — and the Shanghai market took its cue from the Chicago Board of Trade, then the world's pricing center for grain. A single cabled Chicago quotation could thus move the Shanghai board price overnight, as it does here; the bushel (the 60 pounds the text gives, about 27 kg) was the American trading unit, foreign to a market that dealt in sacks. (Corroboration: corroborated.)

Wu Xingya (1892–1936) was a leading figure of the Nationalists' 'CC Clique' and, from 1932, director of the Shanghai municipal Social Affairs Bureau, the organ regulating the city's commerce and labor. He was known for working through underworld connections, and his ties to Du were close — so that a single letter from Du could conjure an official proclamation from his bureau, which is precisely the reach the chapter means to display. He died the same year as these events. (Corroboration: corroborated.)

ch19.anchor: the "Green Warship" brand flour of the Wuxi Maoxin Mill
ch19.note: On the exchange a single mill's brand served as the benchmark against which every other mill's flour was graded and marked down. The 'Green Warship' (lü bingchuan) was the mark of the Rong family's Maoxin and Fuxin mills; the 'Red-and-Blue Cart' was the Fufeng mill's. Because the mills that held this grading power also sat on the exchange's board, it was at once the grievance the interior mills were fighting and the prize Du and Yang meant to seize.

ch19.anchor: Rong Zongjing and Wang Yuqing of the two mills Wuxi Maoxin and Shanghai Fuxin
ch19.note: Rong Zongjing (1873–1938) and his younger brother Rong Desheng (met in an earlier chapter, where his 1946 kidnapping is recounted) built the largest private industrial group in Republican China — the Maoxin and Fuxin flour mills and the Shenxin cotton mills, at their height roughly three-tenths of the nation's flour output. Rong Zongjing was known as China's 'Flour King'; Wang Yuqing was his partner and the mills' general manager. Against such men the gang boss was, for once, the newcomer. (Corroboration: corroborated.)

ch19.anchor: make Wang Yiting lose the election
ch19.note: Wang Yiting (1867–1938; born Wang Zhen) was a comprador for the Japanese Nisshin Steamship line and a director of many Shanghai firms, but famous above all as a painter of the Shanghai School — a disciple of Wu Changshuo — and as a devout Buddhist layman and philanthropist. It is against that public name for charity that the narrator's charge lands: that Wang funded his 'good works' with the exchange's money. (Corroboration: corroborated.)

ch20.note: This article first appeared in 1964, in the seventeenth collection of the Shanghai committee's Selected Historical and Cultural Materials. In reprinting it in 1986 the editors made a few textual changes and folded in, as footnotes, relevant material from a later piece by Pang Jingzhou, 'Corrections and Supplements to "Du Yuesheng and the Heng Society."' The notes below attributed to the source are those editorial footnotes. By the source's own account Pang Jingzhou was a physician and a friend of Du's who, after the war, served as a member of the Shanghai Municipal Council.

A footnote by the source's editors: according to Tang Shichang's recollection the Heng Society was formally established in 1934. The author gives 1932 here and below; the discrepancy is the source's own and is left as printed.

ch20.anchor: Yang Du, Qiu Fangbai and Wang Youtang
ch20.note: A long footnote here, from Pang Jingzhou's corrections, disputes this list. Yang Du (styled Xizi) was never Du's secretary but an honored guest: he and Gu Ao (styled Juliu) had been among the 'Six Gentlemen' who promoted Yuan Shikai's short-lived Hongxian monarchy in 1915–16. For a time Gu Ao would come to Du's house to tell old anecdotes, a water-pipe in hand; Yang Du fell ill after only a few visits, and Du paid his medical and household costs. The note adds that Du made a point of entertaining down-and-out notables of every stripe — in 1931 he staged opera to fete the generals Li Jishen and Chen Mingshu as they passed through Shanghai; in wartime Hong Kong he supplied the warlord Wu Peifu's secretary, the poet Yang Yunshi, with ginseng, medicine and money and paid for his burial; he received the Suzhou elder Zhang Yilin. Du is quoted: 'People always love to be made much of, and so they feel for a man who makes much of others. From these decayed, dispirited old men I look for no repayment; but what I shall get in the end will far exceed the little I so easily lay out now.' Qiu Fangbai's true name, the note ends, was Qiu Fangmo, a Fujian man recommended to Du by Liu Zhilu and Chen Qun. Yang Du and the Hongxian monarchist circle are historical; the rest is Pang's own testimony.

A footnote from Pang Jingzhou's corrections: when Xu Shiying handed Du the order appointing him a standing member of the relief commission, Du at first declined it, saying that to accept would pin him to a single appointed post and cost him all his other usefulness. In truth, Pang writes, though Du affected to make light of office he prized it at heart: living later at the Maoming Apartments he would address Lu Jingshi on the telephone as 'Director Lu,' only because Lu was closely tied to the Juntong and to some degree trusted by Chiang Kai-shek — which drew the ridicule of friends, the private grumbling of his sworn brothers, and the envy of Heng Society men who had not risen so high.

ch20.anchor: chief secretary at the Hong Kong head office of the Chinese Red Cross
ch20.note: A footnote from Pang Jingzhou's corrections identifies the author of this article: Guo Lanxin was the secretary Du engaged when the Red Cross set up its Hong Kong head office, alongside an English-language secretary, an accountant and others, all of whom knew the circumstances of the time at first hand.

ch20.anchor: director of the Public Debt Department of the Finance Ministry
ch20.note: A footnote from Pang Jingzhou's corrections: Bian Dingyuan was in fact chief of the General Affairs Department during Kong Xiangxi's tenure at the Finance Ministry, not of the Public Debt Department.

ch20.anchor: Xu Ziwei, introduced by Qian Xinzhi
ch20.note: A footnote from Pang Jingzhou's corrections: Xu Ziwei, a Wujiang man, had earlier handled documents for Huang Yanpei in the Sichuan-Xikang reconstruction body and the national-salvation bond drive; it was basically on Huang's introduction that Du used him, though in Chongqing Du so often took counsel of Qian Xinzhi that Xu's appointment as branch manager may have had Qian's assent.

ch20.anchor: his disciples Gu Jiatang, Ye Zhuoshan, Pang Jingzhou, Hu Xuwu, Yang Zhixiong
ch20.note: A footnote from Pang Jingzhou's corrections — Pang was himself one of the five — states that none of these men were Du's disciples. Gu Jiatang was Du's sworn brother; Ye Zhuoshan stood a generation above Du in the gang's reckoning; Yang Zhixiong, once a Siemens employee, had met T. V. Soong while out riding in the suburbs and afterward carried messages between Soong and Du; Hu Xuwu was Du's secretary, a cool and retiring man who kept the cipher-book and, in Pang's judgment, served for his salary rather than out of devotion. Pang adds that he himself was no disciple either, having merely come to know Du over gambling around 1926 and fallen under him in a working sense only in 1937–1939, when Pang was secretary-general of the Red Cross and Du its acting head.

ch20.anchor: Miles (deputy director of the Sino-American Cooperative Organization)
ch20.note: A footnote from Pang Jingzhou's corrections: the meeting with Miles was not at Guiyang but at Zhijiang, from which the party flew on to land at Changting in Fujian. Milton E. Miles, of the U.S. Navy, was deputy director of the Sino-American Cooperative Organization, the wartime intelligence body run jointly with Dai Li.

ch20.anchor: lived all along at Gu Jiatang's house
ch20.note: A footnote from Pang Jingzhou's corrections gives Du's postwar lodgings more exactly: after returning in 1945 he stayed at Gu Jiatang's only three or four months, moved to Ninghai West Road for the lunar New Year, and in 1946 took a small flat, No. 705 at the Maoming Apartments, rented in the name of his disciple Xu Maotang. Living with him were Yao Yulan and her sworn-sister Meng Xiaodong; with the rooms few and Du often ill, few were received there beyond Lu Jingshi, Zhu Xuefan and a handful of others, though the boards of the securities and gold exchanges met there to accommodate his illness, and Mei Lanfang, Cheng Yanqiu and Ma Lianliang came to talk over performances. Pang, a physician, names himself among the doctors who treated Du there.

The 'Solitary Island' (gudao): when the Japanese took the Chinese-administered districts of Shanghai in November 1937, the foreign-run International Settlement and French Concession remained unoccupied enclaves — islands of nominal neutrality amid Japanese-held territory — until Japan seized them too after Pearl Harbor in December 1941.

The Cotton and Wheat Loan of 1933: a United States credit of some 50 million dollars, negotiated by T. V. Soong as finance minister, under which China bought American raw cotton and wheat. Soong arranged it around the time of the London World Economic Conference of that year.

ch20.anchor: Sichuan is the homeland of the Paoge
ch20.note: The Paoge ('Gowned Brothers,' also called the Gelaohui): the great secret-society brotherhood of Sichuan and the upper Yangtze, as pervasive in that region as the Green Gang and the Hongmen were in the lower Yangtze. Making Chongqing the wartime capital set the Shanghai gangsters down on the Paoge's home ground.

ch20.anchor: the traitors Tao Xisheng and Gao Zongwu
ch20.note: Tao Xisheng and Gao Zongwu had followed Wang Jingwei into his peace negotiations with Japan and then broke with him: in January 1940 they fled to Hong Kong and published the secret draft treaty Wang had initialed, a propaganda coup for Chongqing known as the 'Gao–Tao Incident.' The author, writing from the Nationalist side's later standpoint, still brands them traitors for their earlier time in the Wang camp.

ch20.anchor: the Zhigongtang and the Three Dots Society
ch20.note: Two bodies of the Hongmen (Triad) tradition, distinct from Du's own Green Gang world: the Zhigongtang, the long-established overseas-Chinese Hongmen fraternity strong in Hong Kong and the Americas, and the Three Dots Society (Sandianhui), a Triad branch of south China.

The title as printed. It is a Peking-opera showpiece of the Flower Cave type, staged so that several leading dan singers appear together as multiplied versions of one character — a heroine and her demon doubles — which made it a natural vehicle for assembling a whole roster of stars at a benefit.

ch20.anchor: the fifteenth of the seventh month
ch20.note: By the lunar calendar. The fifteenth of the seventh month is the Zhongyuan or 'Ghost' Festival, when offerings are made to the dead; Du Yuesheng's birthday fell on that day, so the society's yearly birthday tribute coincided with it.

ch21.note: The narrator was a finance official of the Juntong, the Nationalist military secret service, and later of its successor the Bureau of Confidential Investigation, rising to head the management office that handled its money; his account is thus an insider’s view of the funds that passed between Du Yuesheng and Dai Li’s intelligence apparatus.
The military academy founded near Guangzhou in 1924, with Chiang Kai-shek as its first commandant; its early graduates formed the core of his officer corps and the base of his personal power.
The tewuchu, the secret-service organ Dai Li built up from 1932; it was the direct forerunner of the Juntong, the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Military Affairs Commission.

The Fuxing (‘Renaissance’) clique, better known in English as the Blue Shirts: a militarist secret society of Whampoa officers formed around Chiang Kai-shek in the early 1930s. The rival secret-service networks of Dai Li and of Kang Ze both grew out of it.

The Liangguang (Two Guangs) Incident of 1936, in which the Guangdong and Guangxi warlords rose against Nanjing under the banner of resisting Japan; its collapse let Chiang absorb Guangdong. Corroborated.

The biedong jun, the guerrilla army raised in 1937 from Shanghai’s Green and Red Gang men under Dai Li and Du Yuesheng; it is the same force treated, under the name Special Operations Corps (biedongdui), in the preceding chapter on the Heng Society.
The Zhongyi Jiuguo Jun, the intelligence-run irregular army into which the 1937 gang levies were reorganized; it operated behind Japanese lines in the lower Yangtze under the Juntong through the war.
The source appends an editors’ note to this name: ‘Per Comrade Zhu Xuecang’s recollection this should be Zhang Ye.’
Soong Ch’ing-ling (1893–1981), widow of Sun Yat-sen and a prominent public figure of the left, by the 1930s an outspoken critic of Chiang Kai-shek’s government.
In the Hanoi attempt of March 1939 the Juntong gunmen killed Zeng Zhongming, Wang Jingwei’s secretary and close associate, in Wang’s stead; Wang himself escaped. Corroborated.
Wang Jingwei’s open telegram of 29 December 1938 calling for a negotiated peace with Japan, known as the yandian after yan, the telegraphic code-character for the twenty-ninth of the month.

ch21.anchor: Tao Xisheng and Gao Zongwu's defection from Wang to Chiang
ch21.note: The ‘Gao–Tao affair’ of January 1940: Gao Zongwu and Tao Xisheng broke with Wang Jingwei and made public, in Hong Kong’s Da Gong Bao, the draft treaty Wang had negotiated with Japan. The defection is well attested; the narrator’s account of Du Yuesheng’s brokering role is his own testimony.
Yunong was Dai Li’s courtesy name; Du and his circle commonly called Dai by it.

Wang Yaqiao (1889–1936), the Anhui-born gang leader and anti-Chiang conspirator known as the ‘assassination king,’ behind a string of political killings and attempts. He was shot dead by Juntong agents at Wuzhou; the usual date is October 1936, a month before the one the text gives. The claim that he had been a sworn brother of Chiang’s is the narrator’s.

ch21.anchor: Nationalist Central Party Headquarters in Nanjing
ch21.note: The shooting of 1 November 1935 at the Nationalist party’s Sixth Plenum, when the gunman Sun Fengming, aiming at Chiang Kai-shek, wounded Wang Jingwei instead. The source appends an editors’ note here: ‘One account has this operation organized by Hua Kezhi.’ Scholarship bears this out—Hua Kezhi’s group planned the attack, generally traced to Wang Yaqiao’s circle.

The ‘four big families’ of Nationalist China in Communist usage—those of Chiang Kai-shek, T. V. Soong, H. H. Kung and the Chen brothers (Chen Lifu and Chen Guofu)—held up as the bureaucratic-capitalist clans that monopolized the state’s wealth.
The tripartite body set up at Beiping in January 1946—Nationalist, Communist and American—to oversee a truce in the civil war; it broke down within the year.
The Comintern-run university in Moscow (1925–1930) that trained a generation of Chinese revolutionaries of both parties; Chiang Kai-shek’s son Chiang Ching-kuo was among its students.
The Baomiju, into which the Juntong was reorganized in 1946 under the new Ministry of National Defense; it carried on the same secret-service work under a less conspicuous name.

The cited article is the narrator’s own. The Western names are those of American figures the piece links to Dai Li—among them Patrick J. Hurley, U.S. ambassador to China in 1944–45, and Admiral Charles M. Cooke; the first is left as the source transliterates it.

ch22.note: Zhang's names all play on the tiger. His milk-name Ah Hu (阿虎) means ‘Little Tiger’; the personal name Yin (寅) he later adopted is the third of the twelve Earthly Branches, the one the zodiac pairs with the tiger; and his style-name Xiaolin (哑林) is a homophone of his original given name Xiaolin (小林, ‘little grove’), rewritten with a character meaning ‘roar’ so as to read ‘a tiger roaring in the forest’ — the gloss the text supplies a few lines on. The two Xiaolins sound alike and are written differently.

Ji Yunqing (季云卿, 1868–1939), a Wuxi-born Green Gang boss and one of the senior underworld figures of the Shanghai concessions, who kept teahouses and theaters as a front and dealt in opium, kidnapping and extortion. His career prefigures Zhang's own end: during the war he went over to the Japanese, and in September 1939 he was shot dead by a Juntong agent on Dai Li's orders — the same secret-service reach that would take Zhang the next year. Corroborated by the standard accounts.

Zhang Zuolin (张作霜, 1875–1928), the ‘Old Marshal,’ was the warlord of the Fengtian (Manchurian) clique who dominated the northeast and twice held Beijing; the Japanese killed him in 1928 by blowing up his train. For a Hangzhou gambling tough to model himself on him, and let his followers call him ‘Marshal Zhang,’ is the swagger the passage means to convey.

The warlords of the Zhejiang clique. Lu Yongxiang (卢永祥) held Zhejiang as its military governor (dujun), and He Fenglin (何丰林), his subordinate, was Songhu Defense Commissioner — the officer commanding the Shanghai–Wusong garrison, and so the military power behind the concessions' hinterland. Their patronage is what let the gangs run opium up the river unmolested. The rivalry between this Zhejiang clique and the Jiangsu (Zhili) warlords broke into the open in the Jiangsu–Zhejiang War of 1924, after which Lu and He lost their footing.

The legal-tender (fabi) reform of November 1935: the Nationalist government nationalized silver, took it out of circulation, and made the notes of its four government banks the sole legal money. Advance word of so large a currency move was worth a fortune to anyone placed in the exchanges — which is the tip-off H. H. Kung and T. V. Soong are said here to have passed to Du. The reform is a matter of record; the private tip is the memoir's charge.

ch22.anchor: organized a "New Asia Peace Promotion Association,"
ch22.note: Of the three big bosses, Zhang alone went over openly to the Japanese. Where Du Yuesheng ran resistance-linked relief and intelligence work from Hong Kong and Chongqing, and Huang Jinrong sat out the occupation in retirement, Zhang turned this ‘New Asia Peace Promotion Association’ into a procurement arm for the occupying army and angled to head a puppet Zhejiang government. It is this open collaboration that marked him for death.

ch22.anchor: bought over Zhang's personal bodyguard Lin Huaibu
ch22.note: The killing itself is well attested: on 14 August 1940 Zhang was shot at his own house by his bodyguard Lin Huaibu, a Fujian boxer taken into the household only weeks before. That Dai Li's Juntong had suborned him is the account the Nationalist side put out and the one this memoir follows; but it is not certain. Chen Gongshu, the Juntong's Shanghai station chief, who had himself twice tried and failed to kill Zhang, wrote that he learned of the death from the newspapers and had no hand in it, while Lin's own confession put it down to a private grievance — his wretched pay against soaring wartime rice prices, and a cursing from Zhang. The recruitment is thus uncorroborated at its center, even as the Juntong claimed the credit.

ch22.anchor: director of the puppet Hangzhou Tinfoil Bureau
ch22.note: Tinfoil (锡箱, xibo) is paper backed with beaten tin, folded into mock ingots and burned as spirit-money in worship of gods and ancestors; its manufacture and sale around Hangzhou were a taxed trade, and the Tinfoil Bureau was the office that ran the levy. Under the occupation it became a puppet-regime monopoly — hence the ‘puppet Hangzhou Tinfoil Bureau’ whose director Zhang was entertaining when he was shot.

ch23.anchor: outside the Qiantang Gate of Hangzhou
ch23.note: The two lives of Zhang in this collection do not agree on his origins. The preceding article makes him a native of Cixi whose family moved to Hangzhou when he was twenty; this one makes him Hangzhou-born, of a fallen landlord family outside the Qiantang Gate. They differ, too, on how he first reached Shanghai — the one has him follow the gangster Ji Yunqing there around 1912, this one has him follow the ex-policeman Wu Hong. Standard reference works follow the Cixi account. Both are given here as their authors wrote them.

Doihara Kenji (土肥原賢二, 1883–1948), the Japanese army intelligence officer long active in Manchuria and north China — the ‘Lawrence of Manchuria’ behind the 1931 seizure of the northeast and its puppet state — hanged as a Class-A war criminal in 1948. (Rōnin, literally a masterless samurai, is used loosely here for a Japanese adventurer operating in China.) Nagano Osami (永野修身, 1880–1947), named just below, was the Japanese admiral who later became navy minister and chief of the naval general staff and was tried as a war criminal after the war. That Zhang was cultivating men of this rank as early as the 1920s is the memoir's measure of how high his Japanese ties reached.

ch23.anchor: a tacit understanding with the traitor Yin Rugeng
ch23.note: Yin Rugeng (殷汰耳, 1885–1947), the Japanese-sponsored collaborator who in November 1935 proclaimed the ‘East Hebei Anti-Communist Autonomous Government,’ a puppet regime carved out of the demilitarized zone south of the Great Wall; captured and executed as a traitor after the war. An understanding with him is what let Zhang route Soviet timber into Japanese-held Manchuria.

Wellington Koo (Gu Weijun, 顾維釜, 1888–1985) was the foremost diplomat of Republican China — foreign minister, ambassador to Paris, London and Washington, later a judge of the International Court of Justice; that a Shanghai gang boss could call on him to advance a son shows how far Zhang's reach ran. Chu Minyi (1884–1946), noted earlier in the collection, would become foreign minister of the Wang Jingwei collaborationist regime and be executed for it.

The ninth Panchen Lama (Thubten Choekyi Nyima, 1883–1937), the second-ranking hierarch of Tibetan Buddhism, who had left Tibet in 1923 after a breach with the Dalai Lama and spent his last years in China under Nationalist patronage, preaching and raising funds. He was in Shanghai in 1934 and spoke there that June. He was a patriotic figure who gave to the resistance and urged the cause of national defense — which lends an edge to his being feted by a man then courting the Japanese. Corroborated by the record of his years in eastern China.

ch23.anchor: the traitors Chen Gongbo, Zhou Fohai, Jiang Kanghu
ch23.note: Leading men of the Wang Jingwei collaborationist regime set up under Japanese auspices in 1940. Chen Gongbo (陈公博, 1892–1946), once a founding member of the Communist Party, became the regime's number-two figure and mayor of Shanghai, and headed it after Wang's death in 1944; executed in 1946. Jiang Kanghu (江亢虎, 1883–1954), founder of an early Chinese Socialist Party, also took office under the regime and was imprisoned after the war, dying in prison. Zhou Fohai is noted earlier. Zhang's hosting all three marks his open passage into collaboration.
